label: Mapping Surfaces: The Metric
notes: Spanning printed pages 31 through 50, this chapter asks what data a flat map must carry so that lengths, angles, and curvature can be recovered from the page alone. The answer is the metric, the first fundamental form, and the whole chapter is built around inspecting how it distorts.

label: The Chapter Question
notes: A coordinate grid is only a set of labels. The geometric content lives in how those labels convert into measured length. We motivate the metric by drawing one coordinate cell and asking how its true side lengths and corner angle depend on position, which already forces three local coefficients on us.

label: The Line Element
notes: The first fundamental form packages all intrinsic measurement into one quadratic expression. Given a coordinate displacement, it returns the squared physical length. E, F, and G are dot products of the coordinate tangent vectors, so they vary from point to point and encode the entire shape of the surface as felt from inside.

label: Reading E, F, G
notes: Each coefficient has a concrete job. E and G are squared speeds along the two coordinate curves, while F measures their non-orthogonality. When F vanishes the grid is locally rectangular. We tie every coefficient to a side or angle of the small coordinate parallelogram so the formula stops being abstract bookkeeping.

label: Measuring with the Metric
notes: Once E, F, and G are known, arc length, angle, and area follow by integration without ever leaving the chart. We show the arc-length integral along a curve, the angle formula between coordinate directions, and the area element. This is the payoff: all intrinsic geometry is computable from three functions of position.

label: Tissot's Indicatrix
notes: To see distortion at a glance we map a tiny circle of directions through the metric and watch it become an ellipse. The ellipse axes are the principal stretch factors. A round indicatrix means faithful local shape; an elongated one exposes anisotropy. This single picture summarizes how a map deforms the neighborhood of each point.

label: Conformal Maps
notes: A conformal map preserves angles by scaling every direction equally, so the metric reduces to a single position-dependent factor times the flat form. Tissot's indicatrix stays a circle, only its radius changes. Conformality is the strongest faithfulness a flat map of a curved surface can hope for, and it costs us honest areas.

label: Stereographic Projection
notes: Projecting the sphere from its north pole onto the tangent plane gives the cleanest conformal chart. We derive the projection geometrically by similar triangles, read off the conformal scale factor, and note that it blows up near the pole. The construction makes the angle-preserving property visible rather than merely asserted.

label: Circles Map to Circles
notes: The signature miracle of stereographic projection is that every circle on the sphere maps to a circle or a straight line in the plane. We sketch why a circle, as the intersection of the sphere with a plane, projects to a conic that the conformal scaling forces to close up into a round circle, with great circles through the pole becoming lines.

label: The Mercator Map
notes: Mercator stretches the stereographic idea into a cylinder so that rhumb lines become straight. Demanding conformality on a cylindrical chart fixes the vertical spacing as an integral of the secant of latitude. The same conformal bargain returns: angles and compass bearings are honest, but areas near the poles inflate without bound.

label: The Inevitable Distortion
notes: Because the sphere has curvature and the plane has none, no chart can preserve both lengths and angles at once. Theorema Egregium is the deep reason, previewed here through the metric. Every world map therefore lies in some controlled way, and choosing a projection means choosing which quantity you are willing to sacrifice.

label: Recap: What the Map Must Carry
notes: We close by collecting the chapter's thread: the metric is the intrinsic data, E, F, and G compute all lengths and angles, conformal maps trade area for angle fidelity, and stereographic projection realizes that trade beautifully on the sphere. The metric, not the embedding, is what a faithful map must transport.
